title: Aisha the scholar
hookLine: the companions brought her their hard questions, and she corrected them from the Qur'an and from what she had seen
last: THE ONE WHO MADE HIM SMILE.

lines: THAT IS NOT WHAT HE SAID.
cards: A report is being passed along. It comes from a respected companion, and it says the dead are punished because their families weep for them. Then it reaches Aisha, the Prophet's wife, and she does not simply nod.
In the account in Bukhari, she says, in effect: may Allah have mercy on him, but that is not what the Messenger said. And she reaches for the Qur'an to answer it. Today: Aisha the scholar.

teach.b: Aisha lived beside the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the small rooms next to the mosque. After his death, people came to her door with questions, and the hadith collections keep her answers.
Here is how she answered the report about weeping. She said the Prophet had spoken about a particular person, not about all the grieving.
And she pointed to a principle the Qur'an states more than once: no soul carries the burden of another soul. A family's tears cannot be counted against the one they mourn.

That is the scholar's move: test what you hear against the text, and against what you witnessed. She did it again when some said a woman passing in front of a man at prayer cuts off his prayer, as a donkey or a dog would.

teach.h: YOU HAVE MADE US EQUAL TO DONKEYS?
teach.b: In Bukhari, she answers sharply: you have made us equal to donkeys and dogs. I used to lie stretched out in front of him while he prayed. She was an eyewitness, and she used it.

teach.h: WE ASKED AISHA, AND FOUND KNOWLEDGE.
teach.b: Tirmidhi preserves the words of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: whenever a hadith puzzled them, they asked Aisha, and found knowledge with her. Her nephew Urwa learned from her and taught others in turn.
A later scholar, al-Zarkashi, gathered her corrections of other companions into a book of their own.
So when Muslims speak of the mothers of the believers as teachers, this is a large part of what they mean: a woman at home, with a door that kept opening, and a habit of checking the words.

how: Muslims learning hadith meet Aisha as a narrator again and again, and her corrections of other companions are studied as part of how the early community checked what it heard.

o: the Prophet's wife who taught and checked hadith
the Prophet's youngest daughter, wife of Ali
a woman who compiled the first written Qur'an

games.q: Aisha the scholar — tap the pairs.
p: I lay in front of him as he prayed
we asked Aisha and found knowledge
her nephew, who learned from her

s: Aisha accepted every report she heard about the Prophet
she tested reports against the Qur'an and what she had witnessed, and corrected some.
companions brought their puzzles about hadith to Aisha
Tirmidhi preserves Abu Musa saying they found knowledge with her.
Aisha answered the weeping report with a story, not the Qur'an
she pointed to the Qur'an: no soul carries the burden of another.

games.q: you hear a respected companion's report that the dead are punished when their families weep. you lived beside the Prophet. what do you do?
o: accept it, since the companion is respected.
say he misheard, and point to the Qur'an.
say nothing, to keep the peace.
games.why: in Bukhari, Aisha says that is not what the Messenger said, and recites that no soul carries another's burden.

practice: Think of something about faith, or about this path, that you've heard repeated and never checked: a saying, a rule, a story.

Hold it up the way Aisha did, asking where it comes from and what the text actually says, until the question is sharp and clear, and think of who could answer it: a teacher, an imam, a librarian, a good book.
If you pray, ask for knowledge that helps.

wordCard.voice: Aisha, the Prophet's wife whose door kept opening to questions, and who tested what she heard against the Qur'an and her own eyes. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: her name, Aisha bint Abi Bakr.

carryVoice: Your line: she taught the teachers. Her answers outlived every knock at that door. That's day eight hundred nine.
